utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good morning, everyone. One administrative matter before we hear further from the witness. The list of forthcoming witnesses identifies a witness Jon Sterenberg as being called fairly soon. I think that there's nothing confidential about the identity of that witness, Mr. Stamp -- Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. And we now propose to call him in the last week of this month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that may make a difference. There is a joint Defence motion to preclude his testimony, and that identifies, of course, the fact that he's not officially identified on the 65 ter list of witnesses, but it also makes the point that his statement is not available in the Serb language. And of course that is a basic obligation in a situation like this. This is a case where the Prosecution ought to make a formal written application to amend the 65 ter list, explain the situation in full, and do it instantly so the Defence have time in the usual way to respond to it. We don't want to be rushed into making decisions on applications of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address one other scheduling matter while the witness is coming in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It concerns the order we have for Mr. Zogaj to finish morning to be followed by Mr. Zyrapi. The Defence has pending some request about delaying his cross, and I think we agreed that we would see how went. Mr. Tanic is scheduled to be the next witness and Mr. Haxhiu, Baton Haxhiu, is scheduled on Wednesday. Mr. Haxhiu is in the position that we had with Mr. Surroi. We had a very tight schedule for him and we would like to have him on and of Wednesday if possible, so if we could go out of order. I've addressed that with Defence counsel this morning, but whatever point we are on Tuesday, if Wednesday we could interrupt if we haven't finished cross-examination of Mr. Zyrapi or if we have just started direct of Mr. Tanic, and do Mr. Haxhiu on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I've been alerted to a Defence application in relation to Tanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not going to affect the issue, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. I don't think so, Your Honour. I've been handed that this morning, and that only has to do with whether he's live or live/92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Chamber are certainly happy to accommodate these arrangements that parties can agree informally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence will now continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration that you took at the very beginning of your evidence in this case to tell the truth continues to apply to that evidence today and until it finishes. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zogaj. I'd like to finish up just a handful of areas from my questioning last week. Now, first of all, I meant to ask you on Friday about Ibrahim Zogaj and his three sons. Are you aware of the fact that sometime in March or April 1998, Mr. Ibrahim Zogaj wrote a letter to the OSCE and other international agencies, urging them to investigate the KLA for the killing of his Serb neighbour Djordje Belic?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but in our village there has not been a Serb ever, and I don't know this person that you're mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, as a journalist in 1998 in the region of Malisevo and Suva Reka, did you have occasion to know and/or report the kidnapping of Mr. Ibrahim Zogaj and his three sons by the KLA and the subsequent discovery of their bodies on 6 April 1998 on the Orahovac-Malisevo road?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never reported on this, and I was not aware about this case. He is not from our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. As part of your journalistic duties in 1998 and 1999, did you report about the actions undertaken by the Kosovo Liberation Army involving the killing and torture of ethnic Albanians even once in any other instance?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, because I never heard of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you an active member of the KLA and did you participate in actions undertaken by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never a member, but I followed the situation in the villages very closely, the situation regarding the shelling of the Serbian forces -- by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving on to another topic. In your direct examination, you talked about a man named Milorad Miskovic, whom you then say also has the last name Nisevic. Did you have occasion to see this individual in uniform at any time, either during March or April of 1999 or any time prior?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. When, earlier; and what type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war started, this person had a driving school, and at the same time he also wore a police uniform in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, am I correct that this Milorad Miskovic was, in fact, a state security operative, a member of the RDB?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, at page 3804 of the transcript from your direct examination, lines 2 through 7, you identify Mr. Miskovic/Nisevic, as being well-known, and then you also state that he was the head of the police department in Suva Reka. Now, sir, you know that this testimony by you is false, don't you? Mr. Miskovic has never been the head of the police department in Suva Reka, has he?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. I also said earlier that the functions changed overnight, the functions of the Serbs in Kosova and Serbia, and there have been such cases. Miskovic ordered the killing of civilians in Suhareke, and, as I said earlier, Mr. Sejdi Bytyqi, the history professor escaped the execution. He survived. He was from Semetisht. He was known as Miskovic, Misevic, Misko, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you describe in your statement that you saw on April 1st, 1999, the burning of houses in the Hoxhaj neighbourhood, from the third floor of your house. How far were these burning houses from your house?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 300 to 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You could not see the markings or insignia on the uniformed persons that you claim started these fires, could you?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had some kind of writing on, some marking, such as "police," "policija."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But at that distance, could you see the exact emblems that they had on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that when I was beaten up and I saw that when we moved from one place to another, when we were forced out from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you a very specific question relating to the houses that were burning in the Hoxhaj neighbourhood that you watched from the third floor of your house, which you said was a distance of 300 to 400 metres away. Could you, in fact, see the precise markings or insignia on the uniforms of the individuals that you claim undertook to burn those houses?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Serbs who burned those houses, because they were the ones who burned, who were killing, who were looting and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. I will take that as a "no" and then I will move on. Now, if --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no "no" here; it's a "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, did you see the markings and insignia on their uniforms or not? I've asked you twice; this is the third time.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw the marking "policija" when I was beaten and on the journey when we were expelled. The whole world knows this, not only me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, I understand what you're saying in relation to one aspect of your evidence, but you're not being asked about that. You're being asked whether, when you saw from a distance of 3 to 400 metres away police burning houses, you could see any of the insignia on their uniforms. Now, can you just concentrate on that, because otherwise you're simply causing confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you're asking, but from that distance, it is impossible to see the marking. But during the time that we were expelled we realised that it was the police, the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We understand that, but all you were being asked is a specific point and you've now dealt with it. Thank you. But it's taken a long while to deal with it, and we don't have the luxury of a long time, as you know, in these cases. We're trying to do justice to as many people's complaints as possible, to the situation of as many alleged victims as possible, and it will not help us if you will not address the particular questions that are asked of you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if you turn briefly to another item of your testimony. Specifically, in your second statement on the first page, you describe how your village of Belanica had 80.000 people in it on April 1st of 1999. And then during your direct examination, at page 3790, at lines 8 through 12, you added to that figure that if the two surrounding villages of Landovice and Guncevac is added, then the figure of persons in that area is well over 100.000. Now, first of all, in terms of geographic size, how large are Landovica and these two other villages of Guncat and Ladrovice, as compared to either Malisevo municipality and Suva Reka municipality?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say Landovice. I mentioned Lladroviq, which is clear, and the other one is Guncat, not Guncevac. And on the 1st of April in Bellanice there were about 80.000 people expelled from other villages. And it is true that including other people from other villages the total would be about 100.000, because these people could not come and physically stay in Bellanice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, you've not assisted us, because you've been asked a question about what area was occupied by this very large number of people. How did the area occupied compare with the size of the municipality of Malisevo or the municipality of Suva Reka. Now, can you address that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bellanice was a little calmer from the 20th of March to the 1st of April, and the flow of people trying to escape the massacres came to Bellanice. And there is a big field, the big field belonged to the village, and there was no room for people to stand. The houses were full. I had about 200 people in my house; 200 people from other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I'll move on to the next question, hopefully the point I want to make will become clear even without the witness's answer to my previous question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, it's a very difficult question to be precise about, and that at least was a stab at giving an answer to your question to try and identify the intensity of the occupation of these villages by that large number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And my next question should, I believe, illustrate a very telling point about that description, Your Honours, at least my next two questions I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zogaj, we've heard testimony here from a Halit Berisha, a former head of the municipality of Suva Reka, who stated that the entire municipality of Suva Reka had only 60.000 inhabitants, including Serbs and Roma. Now, are you telling us that your village of Bellanice and the two neighbouring villages had more persons in it on April 1st, 1999, than normally resided in the entire municipality of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to emphasise here that in Bellanice there were people not only from the Suhareke municipality but also from Rahovec and Gllogoc and Shtime, villages of Carraleve, Luzhnice and others. And wouldn't you think that would add up to 80.000 people?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, in reading your various the only other group of people apart from Malisevo and Suvo Reka that you have identified are between 100 and 1.000 people from outside those two municipalities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So the remainder of the over 100.000 would have to be made up from people within Suva Reka municipality or Malisevo municipality. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, they came from those municipalities where they were at risk, and I said these municipalities were Rahovec, Drenoc, Shtime.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, according to the OSCE, Malisevo municipality, which wasn't a municipality at that point but became one after the war, also had around 60.000 people encompassing some of the people from Suva Reka municipality. Now, the question I have for you is: Based upon your testimony, your claim would seem to indicate that the entire two municipalities of Suva Reka and Malisevo were all in Belanica, which geographically was much smaller, and the two neighbouring villages that you have identified. And I want to ask you whether in fact your estimation is a proper estimation or are you exaggerated or embellishing what you saw for journalistic effect?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my notes, Malisheve was a municipality until 1990. In 1990, the Serb politics changed it. It was not a municipality anymore. However, this municipality had about 40 to 41 villages. At that time they -- the municipality had 40.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So my point is that even if the entire population of Suva Reka and the entire population of Malisevo, and even if we take your estimation of people from outside those two municipalities at its highest of 1.000 persons, we still don't come -- that's the only way we come even close to your estimation of well over 100.000. Isn't that accurate? So I'm asking you: Was this figure you quoted of people in Belanica an accurate estimation or were you, as a journalist, seeking to have dramatic effect?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's exact. About 80.000 people were in Bellanice alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on, then. I have just a handful, three more, points, I believe, to make with you. Now, page 7 of your second statement, you say, when talking of the convoy at Belanica: "Without any direction from the Serbs, we turned towards Suva Reka." Now, I'm having a hard time reconciling this with your first statement from 1999, also on page 7, where you claim that the Serb police directed you in the direction of Suva Reka, while directing others in a second direction. Now, these statements can't both be true, can they?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb police entered Bellanice. They were firing their guns, burning the houses, insulting us as Albanians, looting, insulting NATO and America, Bill Clinton, and others. And they expelled us forcibly in two directions. When we divided at the entrance of the villages -- of the village - this is a clarification for you - this happened four or five hours later, the forces came into Bellanice. These were other forces in addition to the first ones that came. So we were stopped there until the forces came in with heavy gunnery and weapons. They also had bulldozers and excavators. So when the Serb forces entered the village, we left and went in the direction of Suhareke. We were the first -- in the first car that set out to Suhareke. And you never asked me the question: Who was killed in Bellanice? How were they killed? How was the population beaten up? You're avoiding these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, I'm getting very impatient about this. It's not your job to tell anyone in this court what questions to ask you. Your job here, as a witness, is to answer the questions that are asked of you. Now, please bear that in mind and we'll make some progress. You are not going to deter the progress of the court. If you insist on doing this any more, I'll terminate your evidence. Don't just nod your head at me. I expect an undertaking from you to answer the questions that you're being asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While talking about the forces in Belanica, and also previously when you talked about the forces in Pecane, in your written statement of 1999, you claim that the two police that grabbed you out of the car for the first time at Belanica were wearing black uniforms; the other day you changed that to blue uniforms. Now, when talking about the attack on Pecane in your statement, you described that the police were not wearing standard uniforms but, rather, uniforms that were black than anything else. Again, I think you tried to change that as well. Now, I want you to explain to me: How it is that, in 1999, you were adamant that these black uniforms were, in fact, the ones worn by the police, and now you testify that, in fact, they were camouflage blue? How do you explain that change in your perception?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said that. However, the Serb police always wore blue uniforms and blue camouflage uniforms. One belonged to the regular police and the other to the special police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, let's have the particular passage from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the 1999 statement, page 3, and it's in that first carry-over paragraph, in the middle of the paragraph, and I quote: "These were not policemen wearing standard uniforms but their uniforms seemed to be with different colours, more black than anything else. They were masked and had painted faces."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Those are your words, Mr. Zogaj, with your signature attached to them, certifying that this was read back to you in the Albanian language and that you understood and that it was correct. Why the change in your perception?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said that. What I think I said was the police, and I might have mentioned the black uniforms regarding the paramilitaries, but not the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I still can't find this, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's the April 25th and 26th, 1999, statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 3 of the English, the top of the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, on top of page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The top of page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The carry-over paragraph in the middle, it starts: "These were not policemen wearing standard uniforms ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zogaj, I think I have just one more question for you. Did you at any point in time accompany KLA fighters when they were engaged upon attacks or actions directed against either civilians, be they Serb or Albanian, or Serb forces at any time during your coverage of KLA activities?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I followed what happened from close up in the presence of the KLA, mostly during the shelling of the Serb forces and the counter-attacks by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thank you for your testimony, Mr. Zogaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zogaj, my name is Mihajlo Bakrac, attorney-at-law, counsel for Mr. General Lazarevic, and I will have some questions for you. First of all, I wish to clarify something. In your first statement from April 1999, you said that on the 20th of March you were in Suva Reka; and that it was a Saturday, as well as that that day the OSCE monitors withdrew from the town. It wasn't easy for journalists to enter the town because after the OSCE withdrew, the population went away as well. Does this mean that the population of Suva Reka left alongside the OSCE monitors; and if so, in which direction?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we just have an exact quotation from a statement where he's supposed to have said the population went away. I have it in the English translation as: "The town was empty."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation in B/C/S is -- comes from: [In English] "The town -- because the town was empty of people due to the withdrawal of observers." [Interpretation] Page 2, second paragraph of the first statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness clarified that earlier by saying that people were indoors; it was the streets that were empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, did part of the population, of the Albanian population, leave Suva Reka alongside the OSCE monitors?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day only the OSCE observers left; the population remained at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the trial before this one, the Milosevic trial, at page 3664 of the transcript, you said that the OSCE mission departure happened on 20th of March, 1999, when they were signaled to leave. I'm interested to hear what you meant by that. Who did they receive that signal from?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were signaled to leave from the special envoy of the OSCE in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that the OSCE observers had to leave that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Actually, you were liaison between the OSCE monitors and the KLA; that's how you know about such things. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know to have said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, this is actually quite an important question, how it would -- how the departure of the OSCE was organised, arranged. And what counsel wants to know is: What's the source of your information that a signal was given for the mission to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One day earlier from the surrounding villages, the OSCE had its seats there in different villages. They left from these villages, and on the next day they left Kosova altogether. We learned this from the media, in the evening of the previous day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The facts, I understand; but your statement in the trial of Milosevic was that the mission left Kosovo on March 20th when the signal was given for the mission to leave. Now, where did you learn that a signal was given for the mission to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, you had no contact with the OSCE mission in Suva Reka or in your village -- well, first of all, was there an OSCE presence in your village?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't a constant presence, but they came to observe what was going on in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with them as a journalist when they came to your village in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Bellanice?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In Belanica or Suva Reka, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bellanice, yes, I had some talks with them. I don't remember when.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The conversations you had with them, was that in your capacity as your village's representative or a KLA representative for that area?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my capacity of journalist. They asked me about the situation in the village, what was happening with the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did they ask about the KLA? Did they want to know about the situation with the KLA from you?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never asked me that question, because I was not a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with some frequent attacks by the KLA on the police and the army at the time? Was that one of the topics discussed in your area, around Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zogaj. To move on. My learned friend Mr. Ivetic asked you about the number of people who were in your village on the 1st of April. You said that there was a meadow. I believe you mentioned that previously, but just so as to confirm that, is that meadow in the middle of your village surrounded by the houses there?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a meadow surrounded by houses. It is -- nobody tills it or ploughs anything in it or builds there. It is alongside the clinic, and at the entrance to the village, there was a mosque which now has been ruined completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, if I understood correctly, the 80.000 people were in that meadow. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the meadow and in our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Your town or your village has about 220 households; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, at that time. Now it has a larger number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, one doesn't need to be a very good mathematician to come up with a total of about [Realtime transcript read in error "430"] 450 people per house to have been accommodated there at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to have said that they were accommodated. Such number was accommodated in each house, 430 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The figure in the transcript is 430, whereas I think I said 400. But it doesn't seem to be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, you said that on the 1st of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a second. Mr. Zogaj, the question was that 220 households, 80.000 people, comes to about 400 persons per household, and you answered that. Now, can you tell us again your answer to that, because I heard a different answer from what I see in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people were staying in the meadow, in the school, in the clinic, and in the households of the village, including the yards. They were full of people, all these places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said earlier in your evidence that there were 200 in your house alone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, when did Serb forces begin shelling Belanica on the 1st of April? Was it at 11.45?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early morning hours, whereas around 11.45 they did enter the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, my understanding was incorrect, although in your statement you say: "On Thursday, the 1st of April, at 11.45, I saw Serb forces shelling Belanica from two directions. They also shelled Thmushina and Belanica." Which one is correct, what you are telling us now or what you stated in 1999, when you said that they entered the village at 11.45 but that they started shelling as of the early morning hours? Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling had started earlier, not only in Bellanice but also in other villages. But they entered the village around the time I mentioned, that is, 11.45, shelling the village all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, as of early morning, they were shelling, and then they entered the village while the shelling was still going on. And I have the Serb forces in mind. Is this correct, as regards your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb forces were shelling the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, you are a journalist, an intelligent person. Can you answer the same way. How long did the shelling last? Did it last for two hours or three hours? Can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over three hours. During the shelling, two people were killed from Reti village of Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In Orahovac; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bellanice. Two people from Reti village, I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, in your evidence, page 3791, line 2, you said that they used all types of weaponry. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, during the three hours of shelling by using all types of weaponry and your village was full, it was packed, there were people in houses, yards, meadows, and only two people were killed as the result of the shelling. Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling initially was directed around the village; then in the periphery of the village, two people, two females, a mother and a daughter, were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zogaj, the targets around the village as well as its periphery, that's where the KLA lines were positioned. Isn't that correct? They were there in Belanica on the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no positions of the KLA in Bellanice. Precisely in Bellanice, there were not such positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, do you know of a person by the name of Gezim Hazrolli?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him only by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, do you know that after you, we are going to have a KLA witness here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this morning the system wasn't up, and I have this in hard copy only. It's an order of the 1st of April, something that we intend to use with the next witness. I wanted to read the first paragraph. It was signed by Bislim Zyrapi. "Establish a defence line - this is the first of April - left of Bllace, Moshe, Thmushina, and Bellanica, and link up with the line of the 121st Brigade at positions that had been predetermined. The forces to be engaged are the 123rd, 124th, and the 125th Brigade of the KLA."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this order? Did you know that there was a line position of the KLA linked up with Moshe, Thmushina, and Bllace?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that these brigades of the KLA were positioned in other places, in Bllace, Golush, in order to penetrate Doberdolan and other places, as well as in Lladroviq, Senek, Ladros, Banja, Lladroviq, and other places; but not in Bellanice. There were no positions of the KLA in Bellanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2: "Form a tactical combat group out of the units that were in movement. Gzim Hazroli is to command the group." Are you telling me that the order is incorrect and what you are stating is?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was correct for leaving the front line, because they could not withstand the large Serb forces and the attack of its artillery. At that moment they withdrew to one, two, three points, as they describe, and they passed through Bellanice to go to calmer places. But in Bellanice, there were no such positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, my learned friend, Mr. Ivetic, read out a part of your statement when you said that without any direction by the Serbs you went towards Suva Reka. On your first -- in your first statement, page 5, first paragraph, you say: "I told the people to get out of the basement and to take their tractors and cars and to use the highway, because if they stay inside the houses the worst could come to them." You actually told the people to leave Belanica. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time people were forced to leave from -- to leave the village. It was at that time that I told the members of my family and the people who were staying with us to leave and go out because we were in danger. And it was there that Agim Bytyqi got killed. He was a mentally retarded person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I don't see the connection between the murder and what I asked you. I assert, Mr. Zogaj, that upon KLA orders you were the one to organise the people and to make them leave Belanica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that the not correct. It is not at all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, the same order by commander dated the 1st of April, commander Bislim Zyrapi in paragraph 3 states: "The population is to withdraw from Belanica and to be put in Guncat. You carried out that part of the order; isn't that correct. And you advised the population to leave Belanica; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to move away from the microphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That was the KLA commander's order for the population to leave Belanica?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA might have given orders to the people to leave Belanica to go to calmer places in case the village was shelled. But it was for that impossible large number of population to go to these two other because they were packed with people. And in Bellanice, after the entry of the Serb forces, they started to force the people to leave, that is, the Serbian police, army, and paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The document you've used will become what, in due course?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just -- if I may just intervene here. It's P2457, so I think it could retain the same number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a few questions. I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zogaj, are you familiar with an event which took place on the 20th of June, 1998, when the KLA attacked the military at Dulje pass? You are familiar with that event because you, together with some other KLA members, were there. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This did not happen at Duhla pass but in Duhel. The Serb forces took up position there every day, and the KLA, after the Serbian forces withdrew from that place, the KLA had mined the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The question is: Were you there with some other KLA members when a mine was laid and when several Serb soldiers were killed? Were you there, together with some members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an improvised tactic used by the KLA. After the attack, I and some members of the KLA went to look at the place. The Serbian forces had withdrawn from that place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you were there. Can I consider this as a "yes"?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the same day, the KLA ordered some health workers in Suva Reka to lock up the outpatient clinic and to leave so as not to assist any wounded soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I heard at that time, after police or soldiers arrived, wounded soldiers or police arrived, the Albanian doctors were not allowed to administer them aid, and the order was given to them, to the Albanians, to leave the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I mistaken, perhaps, if I conclude this from the book you wrote: They closed the outpatient clinic in Suva Reka and left so that they wouldn't have to offer any assistance to the wounded soldiers. Am I correct in assuming this?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Serbs that told the Albanian doctors to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you telling me that the Serbs locked up and told the Albanians to leave?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs told the Albanians to leave because "it's not your job to help these people." I don't know the reasons why they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And they shut down the outpatient clinic; that's what it says in your book.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the Albanians, not for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: "So as not to assist injured health workers --" no, sorry, "injured soldiers"; that's what is in your book.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanian doctors who were working there until that time, from the time the injured or the killed were sent there - I'm not sure - they were not allowed to work there any longer. They were not allowed to offer assistance to them, and this was at the order of the Serbs themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Therefore, this sentence in your book which says: "In order not to assist the injured, the health workers locked up the outpatient clinic in Suva Reka and went away." Therefore, this is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not locked up, the clinic was not locked up, but they did not allow the Albanian doctors to offer assistance to the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, do you have the book there?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have this page. We can put it on the ELMO, if need be, but I believe the witness already clarified it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You think it's clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think -- I don't think there is any point in me going any further. But, in any case, we can put it on the ELMO. That's page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a matter for you, if you think that clarifies it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to move on, Your Honour. I would kindly ask the usher to put this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's nothing showing on the screens yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it either. Your Honour, perhaps I can move on, and maybe we'll deal with this technical issue in the meantime and then we can go back to this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There it is. I am being told that it is on the video channel; not on the ELMO but on the AV channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, can you read for us the fourth paragraph, which is highlighted in yellow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, just read out, please, aloud and slowly the passage which is highlighted. Don't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says this: "The KLA soldiers had placed a surprise mine, a special mine, on the 20th of June at the place where the Serb forces were, and they activated it with some kind of remote."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness read very slowly, please, for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, please read slowly, because there isn't an English translation of this available. Just go back to where you completed the sentence, saying it was a surprise for soldiers and that they the exploded it with some sort of remote, and then read after that, please, but read slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. "The KLA soldiers had placed a surprise mine or booby-trap on the 20th of June at the place where the Serb forces were positioned, and they had activated it with some kind of remote which was a few metres away. This booby-trap in Duhel was placed by the soldiers Destan Zekolli and Suka Naser. And the Serb forces suffered. The Serb police managed to get the bodies of the killed, but it was not sure what their number was. But angry as they were at the clinic in Suhareke, they looked up this clinic and they did not allow the Albanian doctors to participate at that moment and had told them to leave their place of work."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Visnjic, that sounds very much like it was a Serb instruction, as the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. I must have had an incorrect translation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, on to the other questions I have. Am I correct in asserting that the supply of KLA soldiers in terms of weapons was done from Albania and through people working abroad who had tried to help in various ways?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the weapons were brought on horseback, and that sufficient amounts of weaponry were secured that way; that hundreds and thousands of young people went to Albania and back in such a way equipping the KLA with even more modern pieces of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the way they got their supplies, I mean, the KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, who is Xhendet Lezi? Was he one of the KLA commanders?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What was his position within the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a commander in Bllace, KLA commander in Bllace.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was there a KLA brigade in Bljac?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, there was a KLA unit called Lumi, and later brigades were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, am I correct in saying that Xhendet Lezi provided to you, or told you that there was cooperation between NATO and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said in the book is true and there was cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll give your exhibit an IC number, Mr. Visnjic, and it will be scanned into the system.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC104, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were asked a lot of questions about the KLA and their presence. Can I ask you this: You said, in response to one question, that the KLA were not precisely in Belanica. Can I ask you: How far from Belanica proper, that's the village proper, were the lines of the KLA on or about the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately from Semetisht village or the place called Golush, it's about five or six kilometres. From Bllace, it's about five kilometres. It's closer to Banje, four kilometres, and so on the surrounding villages, surrounding villages with Bellanice, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At about midday or in the early afternoon of the 1st of April, 1999, when the people were forced to leave Belanica, were there any KLA in Belanica?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You estimated the people, who were gathered in the field at Belanica and who were in people's houses and various other buildings in Belanica, at about 11.45 on the 1st of April to be in the vicinity of 80.000 to 100.000. How did you manage to make that calculation, to come to that approximation?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time the war broke out in Kosova, people came from Drenoc and Bellanice, then from Rahovec. But after the 25th of March, so on the 24th, NATO bombing started and a number -- a large number of people came to our village from Suhareke, from Rahovec. And on the 1st of April, this number was about 80.000 people in Bellanice only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm asking is whether or not you as a journalist or other persons who were there used any system or any methodology to make an assessment, to estimate the amount of people?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cooperation with the civil staff that was created in the village, in the course of these people coming to the village, and these people were sheltered while they came, and this civilian staff helped these people; assigned them to houses and sheltered them wherever they could. And on this basis, we concluded that the population in our village at the time was about 80.000 people, because this was a very large meadow, the one I talked about. I can bring a photograph of this meadow for you to see how large it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Did the people who were forced out of Belanica on the 1st of April, 1999, go to Guncat?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 1st of April, Albanian people went to Guncat, but the village, the Guncat village was overcrowded. People were staying in the streets. So those who went there with -- in their tractors, they could not go to Guncat; that's why they stopped at Bellanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it, therefore, that the people who were driven from Belanica on the 1st of April did not go to Guncat that day?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not go to Guncat. Belanica is in the centre; it's between Guncat and Lladroviq. And from Pagarusha, you have to go through Bellanice to go to Lladroviq and Guncat. It was impossible for all that number of people to go to Guncat. And that's why the population stopped at Bellanice, although the conditions were horrible. The village was overcrowded. There was no food. People did not have a place to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further in re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, that completes your evidence. Thank you again for coming to the Tribunal to give it and for returning when your evidence was interrupted. That brings your presence here to an end. You're now free to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's next witness is Bislim Zyrapi. I'll just set up and then I'll get back to what his evidence is relevant to in a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He is a viva voce witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Mr. Zyrapi's evidence is to a large extent primarily relevant to Count 4 of the indictment to establish the elements necessary for the Prosecution to prove that there was an internal armed conflict in Kosovo at the time of the commission of the crimes alleged in the indictment. I would also refer to paragraphs 78, 92 to 94 of the indictment, and paragraphs 24 to 28 of the pre-trial brief. The witness will also generally describe the position of areas held by the KLA during various times from 1998 and to the end of the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, on reflection, it would probably be better to break now and then to start with the witness after the break. So we would resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's not bring him in, and we'll be back at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, I'd just like to raise one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bring him in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: As far as I can see, we've only received notification from one counsel as to what element -- what documents might be used in cross-examination with this witness, and that notification is only indicating that a number of documents will be used that has previously been provided by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think the rule is that we have to know what documents are going to be used, and we would request notification. I know there are some documents where there is an outstanding issue, but if any other documents that weren't reasonably disclosed are going to be used, I think we need to get notice of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Like any other issues relating to this witness, any comment is noted, but we can decide nothing until we see the state of play at the end of the examination-in-chief. Good morning, Mr. Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which is now being given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me to address you. Last Sunday, as soon as I received the 68 rule documents pertaining to this witness, I demanded to be given a translation of those documents, and I said to the Prosecutor - I mean I indicated orally to the Prosecutor - that we might be using the same documents. But we cannot receive the translation sooner than ten days from this date; this is what we've been informed by the CLSS. And perhaps this is the problem that my learned colleague Mr. Marcussen wanted to acquaint you with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Cepic. This is a matter we will deal with later. Let's get on with the evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, the first person to ask you questions will be on behalf of the Prosecution, and that will be Mr. Marcussen. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I should apologise to my colleague. It's right. He did indicate that he was going to use the Rule 68 document that was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, would you please state your name for the record, mention your full name.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: My name is Bislim Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I was born on the 9th of June, 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In Studencane village, Suhareke municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I finished the primary school in Studencane village, Suhareke municipality. I finished the high military school in Sarajevo, as well as the high military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when did you finish these two schools?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I finished the primary school in 1977. From 1977 to 1981, I finished the high military school in Sarajevo. The higher military academy, I started in 1987 and finished in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you become a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: After my graduation from the high military school in 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: During your service with the JNA, did you have some trouble with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could you please explain to the Court briefly what that was about.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At that time, we were working to form the military liberation -- the liberation army in Kosova and the tribunal found us guilty and condemned us. There were about 30 officers and non-commissioned officers involved in it. I was sentenced to one year and a half on probation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you serve any time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Albanian army in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: No, I didn't serve any recent term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Marcussen, we've been given a correction which I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The name of the army was the Albanian army in Kosova, not the liberation army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So not the liberation army in Kosovo but the Albanian army in Kosovo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, after you had been found guilty, did you continue your service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, like -- many others like me were condemned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, did you personally continue to serve in the JNA after you had been convicted?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And just to clarify the second half of your previous answer, did others who had been convicted as part of the same process, did they also continue their service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you serve after your conviction, in what unit?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In the same unit I was before, in Lukavice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what kind of a unit was that?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Infantry unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what rank did you have?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I was company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: After that, did you continue with the -- well, sorry, how long did you continue with that company?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: From 1989 up to the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then where did you move?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In April of 1992, I deserted from the JNA and joined the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And why did you desert?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I deserted because I didn't like the way the army was transformed when Yugoslavia started to break up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What, in particular, was it that you didn't like?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: To be more specific, the transformation of the popular army into the Yugoslav army, they changed the insignia, and I didn't like its actions when they started the war in Croatia; and then in Bosnia, I didn't like its actions in the course of these fightings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where did you defect to?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I defected to the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you come to serve in the Bosnian army? Were you accepted in the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: From April 1992 to October 1992, I was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In which unit?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Up to October I was brigade commander, 14th Brigade commander. It was a Territorial Defence brigade in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you given a rank in the Bosnian army at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, we didn't have ranks, but when I was transferred to Central Bosnia, I was stationed in Zenica and then in Novi Travnik. I was brigade commander, Brigade 308. When I left the Bosnian army in 1995, at that time I received the rank of lieutenant colonel, but I didn't practice that rank. In January, I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you left, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In January 1995, I left the Bosnian army and went to Holland, where my family was living. I joined my family there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: While you were in Holland, did you come to meet any members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of 1997, it was sometime in December, when I met Fehmi Lladrovci, who was a member of the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did he have any particular function or position in the KLA, or was he just a member?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At that time he was just a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did that result in you joining the KLA eventually?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: After talking with Fehmi, who proposed to me to join the Kosovo Liberation Army, I accepted his offer, and I was asked to join and left for Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When did you go to -- when did you arrive in Tirana?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: They called me on the phone; Lufti Fetahu was present during the conversation. It was in the middle of March 1998 that I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you came to Tirana, were you given any tasks for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived in Tirana, Xhemajl Fetahu gave me the task of working for training the soldiers, training them to use weapons, soldiers who came from different countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were there also soldiers from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, but mainly Albanians came from various countries of Europe. But they came also from Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could you explain a little more about the training that was given. Was it only use of weapons, or was there also more tactical training involved?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Most of the Albanians who came to join the KLA were not trained to fight. They lacked any kind of military experience, so I trained them to use weapons, but also trained them for technical operations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Tactical operations; correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Up to what level would you say this tactical operational training went, squad level, platoon level? Could you describe the level of training.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The level was mostly of a squad level because they came in small groups, and this is how we trained them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Approximately, how long training did these recruits receive, do you think?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The time was very brief; one week, two weeks. This is how long it lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you initially arrived in Tirana, were you already formally a member of the KLA, or were you only accepted later?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I was not formally a member at that time; it was later that I was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when did you become a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: After the General Staff approved my joining the KLA, my actual acceptance began with the training, but the formal joining was when I entered Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when did you enter Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I entered Kosova on the 28th of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so once you had been formally accepted in Kosovo, what was your assignment, and who was you assigned to in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: After I entered Kosova, I was given the task by the General Staff of continuing training the KLA soldiers in using the weapons for tactical operations, as well as to assess the capacities of the then-commanders of the local and zone staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You were accepted -- were you a staff of the General Staff, or where did you hierarchically belong in the KLA at that time?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At that time I was accepted as an officer for training by the KLA members in the context of the Department of Military Operations as part of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Later on in November did you change to a higher position in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. In November of 1998, I was appointed as Chief of General Staff of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how long did you serve as Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: From November to April -- November 1998 to April 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then what did you do from April 1999 onwards?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: From April 1999, I was given the task of Deputy Minister of Defence responsible for defence policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. So we went through this to cover your background a little bit, so the Court understands who you are. I'd like to go a little bit back in time and go back to the period you were in Tirana. While you were in Tirana, did you hear about the attack on the -- the Jashari compound in Prekaz?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of the attack on the Jashari family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What was the upshot of that attack, if you can describe that, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The attack on the Jashari family marked the beginning of the conflict between the Serbian forces and the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At this point in time, so in March 1998, where were the members of the General Staff located?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At that time, in the spring of 1998, the members of the staff were located -- some of them were located in Albania and some others in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did the KLA at this point in time have general headquarters for the General Staff -- sorry. Did the KLA have a headquarter for the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At that time, as I said, the staff was divided in two parts. It have a headquarter. Part of the staff was based in Albania and the other part in Kosova, so it did not have one single headquarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How did the staff communicate between those who were in Albania and those who were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At that time, the members of the staff moved from Kosova to Albania and from Albania to Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So is that to say that the communication took place by people moving back and forth?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you entered Kosovo in May, the end of May, how would you describe the level of organisation of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At the end of May when I entered Kosova, the level of organisation of the KLA was, as I said, the headquarters was split in two, one in Kosova, one in Albania. In Kosova, it was organised in local staffs and in zones. All of them were active, with the exception of two zones, that of Drenica and Dukagjin. The others were in the form of local staffs, and they were in the process of formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How many zones were there at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At that time, the zones were divided in seven zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you mentioned local staffs. How were those staffs organised?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The local staffs were organised on the basis of villages and neighbourhoods all along the periphery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did -- was there a command structure between the villages, so up to a higher level of the zone at that point in time, in those where there were active zones?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In some places, yes. Some were more active like the Drenica zone and Dukagjin, but the other zones, there were no commands when I entered Kosova. And the process developed more with the passage of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in those zones where there was -- where joint command structure had been formed at a zone level, could you describe the type of interaction that was between the General Staff and the zone command.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: It was very difficult at that time for them to communicate, because, as I said, the staff was split in two. The part that was inside Kosova sometimes commanded with the zone commanders directly, communicated with them directly. But there were -- there was no regular communication between the General Staff and the zone or lower levels of commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And -- so at this period in time, who would -- who would order combat operations?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Well, it ought to have been approved by the General Staff in practice -- in theory, but in practice this did not happen. It was the zone commanders or the zone staffs that generally issued these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to call up Exhibit P2453.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, this is minutes of a meeting at a local operational staff of Dukagjin. Did you have a chance to look at this document before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I did not see this document before, but I can see clearly from the title here, it's a working meeting of the operational staffs in the Dukagjin area. And this meeting, as I said, is a meeting of the General-- local staffs, not General Staffs, local staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know the -- do you know the members of the -- or the participants in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Well, as I can see here present were some people that I know. For example, the first one Smajli is Ramush Haradinaj, because his nickname was Iz. Maxhupi is the nickname of Lahi Brahimaj, the major, majori.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The major, who is he, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Majori, the major, was Selim Veseli. Tetaj is the surname of Rrustem Tetaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Tolaj; do you know him?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Tolaj, I can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Skenderaj?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Skenderi, I can't remember now who this Skenderi was. Dauti is Daut Haradinaj. Faton, this was Captain Faton, Faton Mehmeti. Now I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Bujari?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Bujari, I think it was Bujar Ymeri, if I'm not mistaken. Alia, I remember now. Hajdari, I can't remember. Dula, Nazmi. Nazmiu is Nazmi Ibrahimi. Mala is a nickname, the nickname of Alush Agushi. Toni, I can't remember -- or, if I'm not mistaken, he's Xhelal Hajda. I don't remember who Agron is. Nazmiu, the doctor, I can't remember. And I can't remember who Muhameti was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I think we might have passed -- there's a gentleman referred to as Mustafa, do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I can't remember Mustafa. I can't remember at the moment who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No problem. I'd like us to go to the third page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we need to see the Albanian version on the screen, and if we can go down to the bottom of that page. Yeah, if you can stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The last sentence there, would you read out what Mr. Agroni is saying there, please.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Agron says: "Carry out the project you think and within two days the General Staff of the KLA will respond." This is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So, to your knowledge, at this point in time, there was -- for this particular area, there were communications back and forth between the General Staff and the local commanders. Would that be a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Well, from this you can see that there had been contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a fairly significant difference between the translation we have in the transcript of that statement by Agron and what appears in the English translation of the document itself. The English translation of the document itself says: "Draw up a draft of what you think." And what we heard in court just now was: "Carry out the project you think." I think those are two very different things; one is carry forward with an action and one is just sort of provide a draft of what you think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, would you read what it says against the name Agron in the page before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Agron says: "Do the projects you think, and within two days the General Staff of the KLA will respond."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes, the verb can be interpreted in various ways. It has multiple meanings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that clarify it for you, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, no it doesn't. Because one of them's talking about plans and the other one's talking about action, and it may be important which one it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the word, though, that clarifies it is"project."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The response that's anticipated is to a project.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the project may be to attack a police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you say carry on that project, he's saying go ahead and attack the police station. If he's saying draft a plan to attack the police station, that's something different and that's what our English translation says. My concern is that the English translation should at least reflect what the original Albanian document says, and I'm not sure it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
