utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, can you assist us by telling us whether you understand the statement to refer to a plan for future action or to be a statement that action should be carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I read here, it means a project for the future, that they have to act in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the approval of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, during proofing did you have a chance to read various parts of this document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Just in light of the issue that has just come up, would you -- is it a correct assessment of the document that this really is about the organisation of the General Staff in -- or the local staff in this particular area?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In this document, you can see that the staff of the operational area of Dukagjin is being formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So do you think that what Mr. Agroni is referring to here is about the organisation of the local staff, or do you think it's about operations?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This has to do with the development of the Dukagjin staff, and later on they speak about how the command of the operational zone would look like in the future. You can see it in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Around the time of this document, which is June or the second part of June 1998, what was the military situation like in Kosovo, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: You mean in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At that time, in June 1998, from the point of view of the KLA, the KLA was not at the required level of development and organisation, both at the local staff level and the general level. It was not well organised. It was more guerilla organisation than a regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what, in terms of the -- of operations were there combats in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: There was fighting in June and July. In June, there was fighting in Dukagjin and also in the Drenica zone as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How would you quantify the fighting? Was it intense fighting? Was it sporadic fighting? How -- if you can try to quantify it in the areas where there were fighting.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In June, it was not intensive. There were sporadic, small fightings, not very high intensity, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did that situation change later on?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. The situation later changed. In July, August, and September the fighting intensified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Why did the fighting intensify?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In July, the Serb offensive started against all the territories where the KLA was in control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so are you saying that at that point in time the KLA was fighting a defensive war?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In July, yes, they were conducting a defensive war. Earlier, there was some attacking as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is it possible for you, in general terms, to describe the situation through August and September?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The general situation in August and September could be described as fighting in the area where the KLA was in control. The Serb forces carried out an offensive in Drenica and other areas. So there was intensive fighting in these territories. I was there until September, but I think that the fighting continued until the end of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you have described a process where there was an escalation from July to August. Was there further escalations through September and October, or was it mainly a continuation of what had started in August during those two months, September and October?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: September and October were a continuation of the fighting that started in August and even in July, July and August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: During this period through the autumn of 1998, did the role of the General Staff change?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In spring 1998 and up until the end of 1998, the role of the General Staff changed, because the more the war intensified, the more the staff took up roles, as a proper General Staff in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then you left, you said, Kosovo in September of 1998. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In September 1998, I left Kosova and went to Albania on a duty trip, assigned by the staff, and I stayed there until November, when I went back to Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you went back, was that after you had been appointed Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: No. After I returned, I was appointed as Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who were the other members of the General Staff at that point in time, December, January 1998 -- well, December 1998 or January 1999?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: From November until January, the composition of the General Staff was this: The Commander of the General Staff was Azem Syla, until March 1999; then this function was given to Sulejman Selimi, until May 1999; Deputy Commander of General Staff for operations was Sokol Bashota; Deputy Commander for Political Affairs was Jakup Krasniqi; General Inspector, Rexhep Selimi; Military Court, Sokol Dobruna; Department for Personnel Affairs, Adem Grabovci; Department of Intelligence Affairs, Kadri Veseli; Department for Operational Affairs, I was responsible for that, but then Selim Veseli took that function from April and on. Rram Buja was head of the Department for Military Affairs; Political Department, Hashim Thaqi; the Department of Military Police, the responsible person was Fatmir Limaj; Communications Department, Muse Jashari; Financial Department, Lahi Brahimaj. Then another department was created in March. It was the Department for Education and Training; responsible for that was Ekrem Rexha. As far as I remember, this was the composition of the General Staff at that period. I think I forgot to mention the Finance Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you have a chief for logistics; and who was it?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think I forgot that one. Xhavit Haliti was responsible for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And G6, Civil Administration, did you have such a unit?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. Rram Buja covered that, Military and Civilian Relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, this structure of the General Staff - in particular, a division into personnel, intelligence, operational issues, logistics, finance, civil administration, political issues, communications - is that a fairly common structure of a General Staff, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. This was an ordinary structure that a General Staff would have anywhere; the KLA had the same structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so the Directorate for Operational Issues, is that normally known as G3?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So you had that sort of standard structure. What were --

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What were the priorities of the General Staff when you became appointed as Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: With my appointment as Chief of Staff, my priorities were training and education of the members of the KLA, especially the training of the commanding staff from the level of the squad to upper levels, to the brigade, offering them adequate training for them to be able to carry out operations in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where was the General Staff located at this point in time, in November 1998?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The General Staff, from November 1998 until March 1999, was located in the Berisha mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe -- did you have a headquarters? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. There, in the Berisha mountains, there was a headquarters there. I was there with a number of other members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could you describe the organisation -- I'd like to explore a little bit the organisation of that headquarters. Apart from the senior officers, the members of the General Staff, did you have other officers assisting you in your work?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it depended on the department. Each department had a number of people that were involved, and I couldn't tell you an exact number of how many people were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In terms of the infrastructure, did you have, for example, a communications room?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, there was a communications room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in that communications room, or in connection with communication, would there be a duty officer assigned?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, there were duty officers. These were officers from the operational department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what was their role, if you could describe that to the Court, please. [Realtime transcript read in error "The role of the duty officer..."]

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The role of the duty officer was to contact the operational zones, learn about their requests, and transmit these requests to the staff, but also have a clear idea of what was going on in the whole territory of Kosova?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would they keep a log of communications, for example?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. There was a communication log. The communication -- forms of communications were different depending on the possibilities through satellite, telephones, radios, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a transcript issue that is important, I think. It's on page 50, line 24. The question ends with the word "please." And the sentence beginning "The role of the duty officer ..." is an answer, not a question. Line 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I note that. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to talk a little bit about the internal organisation about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we could see Exhibit P2449, please. We can just zoom out a little bit, so the witness can see a bit more of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, this is an attachment to your statement. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This is an interim rules on the organisation of the internal life of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is that a document that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I can see this is dated in Pristina, 1998. Now, if you know, what was the basis for the creation of this document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: There is a preliminary document which was prepared at the end of 1998. This document regulated the organisation of the internal life. In order to prepare this document, we looked at the rules of the Western armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was this document updated since the version that we are looking at now?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. With the passage of time we made changes to it; we updated it. Like, for example, the greetings, the saluting, and other things which time required us to change, depending on the further development and growth of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we go to page 6 of this document, please. And, sorry, that's my mistake. We need to go back to the e-court page 5. Can we zoom out just a little, one click. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, could I -- can you see this article on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. This paragraph is about giving and receiving orders. Would it be correct to say that this is a reflection of the doctrine of command and control; that commanders issued orders, they have to be implemented by subordinates, and they have to report back that orders are completed?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So -- so this basic military principle was applied by the KLA. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember that from the time I was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This rule book, who was it given to?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This book of rules was printed in many copies and sent to the zone commanders, and they were responsible for making it known to other lower units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And we can maybe prepare the next exhibit on the list that I have given to the court officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, this rule book would have been available to commanders in all zones. What about commanders further down, such as brigade or battalion levels?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. It was made available to the battalions, brigades, up to the lower units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How -- so also at the company level, maybe, or platoons, would they have it? Or even further down?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, up to the lower levels, as I said, the squads, for them to have it and read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we could now see Exhibit P2461, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, we talked about command and control and reports a little bit. Do you have a document before you now on the screen, a new document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This document, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is that a document that was provided to you -- sorry, provided from you to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where did you have -- where did you get the document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This is a document from the archives of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you retrieve the document from there?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we can scroll down maybe first of all to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Down here there's a stamp and your name and a signature. This is a document issued by you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we could then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you generally describe what this document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we can scroll up in the meantime so that we have paragraphs 1 and 2 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an order issued to the zone commanders who should report in the daily briefings on the time during which they will report from what time to what time; and then the way of reporting in extraordinary cases when the -- when the opponents moves, to report immediately through these telephone numbers. They were satellite phones which were available at the duty officer, the deputy commander of the General Staff, and the telephone I had at my disposal, and the way the reports should be compiled, how the reporting should be done on the movements of the enemy, the operations. The proposals for decisions, requests to the General Staff, and their reporting on eventual operations and casualties resulting thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is your order that a certain standard format had to be used for the daily -- well, for reports made up to the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was linked to that part of the book of rules on how they should report to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And we have a translation available, so I don't think we need to explore that in more detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to the next exhibit, which would be P2448, please. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, this document, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe we need to zoom out just a little bit for the witness to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You recognise the document. I can see you nod.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This is a document -- this is an order, actually, on not exceeding the powers, and about disciplinary issues. This is an order issued by me to the operational zones of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Again, we have a translation available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But what I'd like to ask you is: What was the background for the issuance of this order?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I issued this order because at that time, and even before I took over that duty, I had received several complaints from the zone commanders, from the soldiers, from the civilian population of maltreatment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: -- of exceeding of powers of officers and soldiers. So I deemed that this was very important for me to issue this order to discipline the soldiers and the commanders, and for them to know a code of conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe this is a good juncture to deal with a related issue. Have -- during the time you were an officer -- an officer in the KLA, did you hear of any crimes being committed against civilians by members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I have heard opinions being expressed, but I was not formally informed. As I said, I heard when I visited people on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We're hearing a siren, but I think it's just a normal Wednesday lunchtime indication. So unless case the Court want me, I'll just to carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The week's passing very quickly, Mr. Marcussen. I'm delighted to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's what happens when you work on weekends, I guess. It's a normal Monday, but we will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you hear about liquidation of people considered to be collaborators?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I have heard such opinions being expressed, that there have been such instances. Even though, as a military person in a superior position, I knew very well that you cannot call someone a collaborator if he's not -- he or she is not taken to a military court and been investigated. At that time from what I heard, there had been such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to just deal a little bit more with disciplinary matters. Could sanctions be imposed for breaches of disciplinary rules?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who could impose such sanctions?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The person who could sanction such disciplinary rules were -- began from the zone level up. They reprimanded the soldiers orally or gave them written critics or even sentence them to short time of detention or even refer them to the General Staff and to the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in instances of disciplinary -- sorry. In instances of breaches of disciplinary rules, at least if they were more serious ones, would reports be made?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The zone commanders in their reports should mention the disciplinary measures taken against those soldiers or commanders who might have breached discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would records also be kept in the personal files of such soldiers or officers?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit P2463 now. Now, again we have a translation of this document. It's an order requesting the military police to assist an investigation or an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, this document, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is that a document that was provided to you -- again, sorry, from you -- or provided by you to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did you get this document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I got it from the archives of the Pashtrik operation zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I think we can just move on to the next one -- to the next document, which is P2464 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that. Mr. Zyrapi, what does the reference to the investigating judge mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an order issued by the military court given to the investigating judge to investigate a serious breach. I don't remember at this moment what it was about, but this is one of the requests that is for the investigating judge to go to this zone and conduct investigations. This refers also to the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who was the judge referred to in this case appointed by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was appointed by the military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By "military court," do you mean the KLA's own military court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'll get back to the office of the military court just in a bit. He was mentioned in the list of members of the General Staff that the witness gave earlier on. But I'll explore that after this next exhibit. I don't know if we have the next one up. Could we have P2464, please. Oh, there it is. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, again -- no, sorry, this we don't have a translation of yet. Mr. Zyrapi, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Again, is it correct that this is a document provided from you and you collected this in the same place as you collected the other document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was taken from Pashtrik operation zone archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could you just explain the Court what this document is.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This document is about a disciplinary breach by a soldier who is recommended to be detained for four hours -- for 48 hours, and the order should be immediately executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think this document is not in Albanian but in Serbian; why is that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The order is in Serbian because the soldier is of Bosnian ethnicity, and it is written in his language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could we see the second page of this exhibit please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is this a handwritten version of the same order but in -- in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. It is the same order. This is handwritten in Albanian. It is a translation of the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, all this has just been to show something about the infrastructure and the organisation of the KLA in disciplinary matters. I'd just like to go back to the military court --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me for interrupting and I might be remiss here. Do we have an English version of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not have -- I just wanted to -- I thought so. We do not have an English version of this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So I'm trying to follow as much as I can, but we do not have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but you do have a Serb version. You have Mr. Visnjic, and therefore I thought it would be unnecessary in this instance to mark this for identification. I thought this is one we could cope with without undue formality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yeah, that's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. That was also my thought, but I should have made that clear, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The military court. Now, you said earlier that on the General Staff, there was Dobruna, who was head of the military court. Did he have any legal training, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Mr. Sokol Dobruna was the main person in the military court. By profession, he is a lawyer and he has experience in this regard. He has quite a lot of experience in justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And was he assisted by any staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: To my recollection, yes, there were three other assistants. In every zone, there was an officer responsible for legal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where would the court sit?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it depend -- it would sit depending on the circumstances, wherever it was called for it to sit, but mostly in the Berisha mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know whether it had regular -- regular sessions, or would it sit on an ad hoc basis when there was a need, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it depended on the circumstances, where the need was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to just explore another related area, the Geneva Conventions. Do you know whether the Geneva Conventions were disseminated in the KLA or distributed?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: To my knowledge, when I joined the KLA, the Director of the Department for Military Affairs, who was Rexhep Selimi at that time, told me that he had distributed some booklets by the Red Cross, which included all the rules of warfare and the legal rules applying to them, which he had distributed to operational zones and to commanders of smaller zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When training was given to soldiers and officers, was there any training or information about the laws of war and the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: As I said, during these trainings, even though they were short-term trainings, apart from the military training we gave the soldiers, we also trained them on the laws of war and the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was that training and information, was that given by KLA staff, or were there anybody from the outside assisting from time to time?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In the course of the training, the training was carried out by members of the military court, but also people who came from outside, people who dealt with the International Red Cross, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you had become -- when you had become Chief of Staff, would have meetings with the zone commanders?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: From January to March, we had frequent meetings every fortnight, I would say, with the zone commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And apart from the zone commanders and you, who would participate in those meetings?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In addition to me and the zone commanders, present was also the deputy commander of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And maybe we can prepare the next exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When these meetings were held, prior to those meetings did you receive any written reports from the zone commanders?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: When the zone commanders came to meet me, I received written reports. Sometimes they would report to me orally and then submit the report later in writing, but generally the reports were in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And were minutes taken of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we could see now Exhibit P2460.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, this document, is that one you recognise?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, again, is that a document that you had provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where have you received that document from?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: From the General Staff archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is this an example of minutes taken from a meeting between the General Staff and the zone commanders?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document which has been compiled after the zone commanders had submitted their reports in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We also have a translation of this document, so I'm not going to go through this. But I'd like to ask you, there are a number of headings in this report; leading and commanding, combat moral, training and mobilisation matters of personnel, logistics, defence and safety, combat situation, reporting on enemy forces and KLA forces, and proposals for tactics and operations. Was this a standard format of the reports of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. This was a general, standard format that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so this reflects a standard, general format you had during these meetings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move into a slightly different area, so if this is a good time for a break, then maybe we can take it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, we have to have a break at this stage for about half an hour. The usher will show you where to go while we have the break. Would you please go with him now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, I'll move into an issue related to the one about meetings where we left off, but let's talk a little bit about planning and ordering of combat operations. Once the structure of the KLA had been more formalised in November/December 1998, whose responsibility was it to order combat operations?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At the time when the structure was stabilised, this competency was of the General Staff. So I had that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Prior to such operations, how -- what would be the planning process of the operations? Could you try to outline that for us.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Could you ask the question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Before ordering a combat operation, how would the planning process be, if you can describe that? For example, did you meet with zone commanders, or how was the planning taking place?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The procedure was like this: First of all, we discussed within the General Staff, and the zone commander of the relevant zone for which this operation was prepared was also asked to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then what would the next step be?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Then after everything was precise, the approval of the General Staff was given to the zone commander to carry out that operation in the zone where he was operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the zone commander would then implement the order through more detailed orders. Is that how I should understand it?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. The zone commander would act according to the instructions contained in the order about the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: During the period from, say, December 1998 to the beginning of the NATO bombing, could zone commanders, on their own, order combat operations?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The zone commanders could give orders on their own if they were attacked in their zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We'll get back to the military situation after the NATO bombing started. But after that point in time, was it still possible for the General Staff to order command operations -- combat operations, or did the zone commanders have more discretion after the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. After the 24th the NATO bombing started and there was a Serb offensive as well, so it was impossible to meet the zone commanders. We used to communicate with satellite telephones or Motorolas. But if we could not communicate, the zone commander could give orders and command operations, but at the first instance when they could contact the General Staff they had to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to now move into sort of more practical structure of the KLA and moving down to the bottom of the organisation, so to speak. How many soldiers did the KLA have during the time you were Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: During the time I was Chief of Staff until March 1999, the KLA had approximately 17.000 to 18.000 soldiers in the territory of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Those soldiers, were they all - how should I put it? - full-time soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Not all of them were full-time soldiers because there was not enough equipment to go around, so many people were dealing with logistics issues and supplies, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Above the level of the -- how were the individual soldiers organised? What was the first sort of unit up from the individual soldier?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: So there was the individual soldier; then the squad; then the platoon, the platoons in a company; then battalions, brigades, and zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The squads of the KLA, how many people did you have in those?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: It depended on the size of the brigade or the battalion or the company. A squad would have three to five soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And a squad, how was -- a squad would receive its order in what form, oral or written?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The squad received its orders from the platoon commander. The platoon commander received his orders from the company commander. I would think that the squads received their orders orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the KLA platoons, how many members did they have?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Again, depending on the size of the battalion or the brigade, a platoon would have 15 to 30 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who appointed the commanders of a platoon?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Platoon commanders were appointed by their own commanders. So they were proposed by the company commander, and then the zone commander approved that proposal. So I'm speaking about this period from December to March. The people who were appointed platoon commanders were people who had been pointed out as very good soldiers during their training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then a step up, how many platoons did you have in a company?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Again, depending on the size of the brigade, there would be three to four platoons in one company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is that slightly smaller than the number of platoons often found in regular armies?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Because it was still developing. It was in the process of growth, and it depended on the number of people that the unit itself had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the company commanders, who appointed them?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The company commanders were proposed by the battalion commanders, and then the zone commander approved their appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then if we go through the same with the battalion, how many companies did you have in the typical battalion?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: It depended on the size of the brigade. There would be three or four battalions. There are -- there were some other platoons in the brigades that dealt with logistics issues as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. If we just go back to the battalion. How many companies did you have in a battalion?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Three to four companies in one battalion. As I said, there were some specialised platoons attached to the battalions that dealt with logistics, communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And again, the battalion commanders, how were they appointed?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: They were proposed by the brigade commander and approved by the zone commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did the battalions have headquarters?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. They had a commander of the battalion, a deputy commander. There were other deputies that dealt with issues of logistics and communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So did the structure at the battalion level mirror the structure of the General Staff, G1 through G8?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: No. It was similar to the brigade structure, so there were not so many departments or directorates within the battalion or the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At the battalion level, were there military police attached at the battalion level?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Not at the battalion level, no, there was no military police attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we move up then to the brigade level, now let's go through the same exercise. How many battalions did you have per brigade? I think you mentioned it before, but let's just take it here again.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Well, the brigade would have three or four infantry battalions, and then specialised companies within the brigade. For example, the special intervention company, the logistics company, a unit for the support of communications issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so the -- for example, the special intervention company, what size would a company typically have?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: It depended, but generally this would be a platoon. That would be the size, because different brigades had different number of people that were attached to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We'll soon move to the next exhibit, so maybe we can prepare that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The special -- these specialised companies of a platoon size, what were their functions?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Well, they had the duty to intervene -- rapid intervention in the areas where there were attacks. They would observe the situation on the ground, the movement of the enemy. This was generally what these companies would do, in addition to other duties given to them by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now if we could see Exhibit P2458, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is it correct you have provided this to us, to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where did you get this document from?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: From the archives of the command of the operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We have a translation of this document with an awful lot of numbers in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the zone commander to the brigade. It gives here different quarters of where these brigades would be operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It was translated as "different quarters." Is it, for example, the 121st Brigade, what we see is the coordinates or points which give the boundary of the zone of responsibility of the brigade. Is that how it works?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Each of the brigades you have number 121 here, 122; and here are the coordinates of the area of responsibility for each brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we can move to the next exhibit, P2465.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And while that comes up, who appointed the commanders of the brigades?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The brigade commanders were appointed by the General Staff at the proposal of the zone commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And once again, is this a document that you have provided to the Office of the Prosecutor, the one that's now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And now we do not have a translation of it, so I guess we should have it marked only identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the commander of the operational zone. This is the proposal he has made for appointing a brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so that proposal would have gone to the General Staff, to you, in other words, would it?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember this particular recommendation and whether you approved it?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this particular proposal. This proposal was not approved by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At the brigade level, apart from the different battalions and special units and logistics units and so on and so forth, was there military police attached at the brigade level?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, there were units, platoons of military police attached to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the full extent of the document, one page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's my -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you don't just want to get the witness to read it and resolve the question of translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, if we -- we can do it that way, then that will be easier for everyone I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, could I ask you to read out the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I guess we have to scroll up a little bit so we get the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We have at the top the emblem of the KLA and then we have some text there giving a date and reference numbers, and we can jump over that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we know it's the operational zone of Pastrik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can we just read the text, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, who is the document from and who is the document to, if we could deal with that first?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The document was written by the operative zone of Pashtrik; at the time it was Ekrem Rexha. At that time it was to appoint and transfer -- this was addressed to the General Staff, pursuant the rules and regulations of the General Staff of the KLA, with the aim of increasing combat readiness of the units. "We propose as follows: Selim Krasniqi, born on the 6th of 10th, 1949, in Prizren municipality. Until now in Brigade 125, proposed to become commander of 125th Brigade. "Number 2, Nehat Basha born on the 24th of 1, 1963, born in Hudanovs, Gurash municipality, or Kamenica municipality. Until now commander of the 125th Brigade, proposed to become Chief of Staff of 125th Brigade." And this document has been issued in two copies; one copy goes to the Chief of Staff of the KLA and then the other copy goes to the archives of the operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then there's a signature block which says the name of the commander and the stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the stamp of the zone and Commander Ekrem Rexha, and below it, it's his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you briefly describe the structure of the headquarter at the brigade level. What kind of facilities did they have, communications?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The brigade command at that time communicated with Motorolas or radio communication. Another way of communication was through couriers or directly with the zone commanders. They did not have any other means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But at this level there would have been -- we can see, for example, an archive. I guess that follows from the document we've just seen. Would there have been a duty office, like the one described at the headquarters level, taking care of communications?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We had the archives, the zones had their own archives where they kept all the minutes or the orders issued. There was also an archive at the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I'd like to move on to the zones. Now, did you still, at the time when you were Chief of Staff, have seven zones, operational zones?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, there were seven operational zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to show now Exhibit P2469. And as we -- it might come up very small. I'd just like to distribute a print of that exhibit to the Defence and the Judges. If the document hasn't come up on the screen, I can give my document to the witness. We're not going to go through this in great detail. I just thought it might be handy to indicate approximately where the zones were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, does this reflect, approximately, the boundaries of the different zones during your time as Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, approximately, the map shows the boundaries of the operational zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, just so we have the right understanding of this, did the KLA hold the entire territory within each zone?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: No, no. Only a very little part of each zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is there a way to generally describe the areas that were held by the KLA? Were you mainly in the mountains, on the low ground? Can you generally describe where you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a point where leading just goes a little too far. I think it's been going on a lot. I haven't said anything, but that goes a little far, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let me just see if the non-leading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Go back to your first question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe the nature of the areas that were held by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Mostly the zones held by KLA were mountainous areas. It was there where it held control, mostly. There were also some non-mountainous areas under its control in Dukagjin territory, Malisheve, and other lowlands. But, as I said, most of its control -- of its territory was in the highlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In the areas where you also held lowlands, what zones were they on this map, the numbers of the zones?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The lowlands were mostly found in the Malisheve municipality; some in Dukagjin, in Gllogjane, which included Barani valley. They were the lowlands. The remainder was mostly highlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so what zone numbers were the ones where you had also lowlands, if you look at the map?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Zone 3, 1, 2, where there was an overlapping of responsibilities between two communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At the zone level, who appointed the zone commander?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At the zone level, the commanders who were appointed by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Orders to and from -- sorry, orders from the General Staff to the zone, would they be oral or written?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: They were both oral and written, but they were always accompanied by written orders when they were oral.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you explain that, please. So an oral order is issued and then you're saying it's followed up by a written order, or how should we understand this?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, they were followed up. Let's say, if an order was given orally, directly to the zone commander, then it was followed up by a written order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And orders going from the zone commands down to the brigades, how would they be, oral or written?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Most of them were written, but there were also oral orders, depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in the case of oral orders, would they also be followed up by written orders or not at that level?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: On this level, when there were oral orders, they were followed up by written orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were there also military police units attached at the zone level?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just for the purpose of illustrating some types of the documents that were -- and records that were kept at the zone level, I would like to run through a series of exhibits, and the first one would be Exhibit P2450.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, has there already been evidence that there were military police units at a lower level or at a higher level?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We have had at the brigade level, and we will get to the General Staff level in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is one of those documents where we do have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But, Mr. Zyrapi, could you explain to the Court what this document is.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This is a document that reflects the general data of a soldier that has joined the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where would these kind of documents be kept?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Usually, such documents were held in the operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the second-last line of handwriting, I see this is from the 15th of May, 1998, so at that level, from what I understand from your earlier evidence, this would have been held by the local commander at that time. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I know this is leading, but I hope it's okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. It's issued by the commander who was then appointed, Mr. Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we could see the next exhibit, P2451.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, what is -- what is this document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This is a document of the Dukagjin operation zone, and it is about dispatching reinforcements to Vuksh village. And you see the names of soldiers being sent there as reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And a similar kind of document, if we could see P2452. Again, we have a translation of it, but if we can zoom in a bit on the, sort of, body of the document. Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This document is issued by the same zone, and it is about the re-assignment of a soldier -- of a commander on the request of the operation zone. He is re-assigned; this officer is re-assigned to the unit in Dujaka village, and it is signed by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could we have Exhibit P2466, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, this is one of those documents where we don't have a translation. Maybe we can deal with it in the same way. Could you first please describe what is this document.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the Pashtrik operational zone. It's an order to mobilise materiel means in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could I ask you -- could I ask you to read out this document from the place where it says: "Order," -- I think it says: "Order for mobilisation ..." And then read the document out for us, please.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: It's an order for mobilising materiel means. It's sent -- it's addressed to the logistic sector of this operation zone "to mobilise four power generators, 220 watts or 50 HZ, two in Peqan and two in Semetisht village. Number 2, for each person from whom these means are taken, he should be given a certificate that these generators were taken away from him. Responsible for implementing this order is the chief of the logistical sector of the Pashtrik operation zone. This order takes immediate effect." It is done in three copies. One is sent to the chief of logistics, one to the archives. It is signed by the commander of the zone, Ekrem Rexha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would -- does this order reflect how equipment would be mobilised by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. This document reflects exactly the way the -- such means were mobilised when I was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we move on to the next document, which is P2467. Sorry. I should probably come up with a formal ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The last document we saw, the one we just talked about, the mobilisation of generators, is that a document that you have provided to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where did you get that document from?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. I got the document from the archives of the Pashtrik operation zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Is that the same with this document we have before us now on the screen? Is that a document you had given to the OTP and collected in the archive yourself?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, do you not have enough documents translated to enable you to conduct your examination with translated documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We really are putting these documents in simply for the purpose of illustrating the kind of records and the level of organisation of the KLA at the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's why I ask you the question. Do you not have enough translated to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No -- well, I mean, what we have is I think what the witness can speak to is this. But I'm coming to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I have this and one more document. Maybe in the interests of time, this one we should ask for a translation of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But, Mr. Zyrapi, could you please tell us what is this document about.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This document that you -- we see here reflects an order whereby two candidates are sent for training as commanders of battalions to a course organised by the General Staff of the KLA. Number 2 shows the data of the candidates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we can scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where -- how many documents -- how many copies was this document issued in, if you look at the bottom left?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: It was issued in two copies; one sent to the brigade commander and to the Chief of the General Staff of the KLA and to the archives the operational zone. And it was signed by the commander of the zone, Ekrem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we could now see P2468 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This one will be marked for identification and you'll have a make a written filing with the translation in due course before it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We will do that I think, rather than spending court time reading out the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this particular document will be automatically admitted once that happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, this next exhibit consists of a number of very similar-looking pages as the one we see on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, what is it we see on the screen here?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: We see a certificate which proves that documents and orders issued by the Pashtrik operation zone are accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And who have accepted them?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: They were accepted by the brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I'm sorry that we don't have a translation of this, but could I ask you just to read out what this says, as it is so short.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Pashtrik operation zone. The date is 10 January 1999. "Certificate to accept the order number 02/1; then 28, dated 10 January 1999, issued by the Pashtrik operation zone. Accept Brigade 121." It's not signed because, it hasn't accepted it. Then you see the other brigades, 122, 123, 124, 125, which have signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I propose to tender just this page of this exhibit, and we'll leave the other pages behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zyrapi. Now, I'd like to ask you a bit about the other assets that might have been attached to the zones. We've heard from another witness in this case that he attended at a KLA military hospital -- at a military hospital. Did -- at what level were -- well, first of all, did the KLA have military hospitals indeed?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. It did have field military hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And under whose immediate command did they fall?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: They fell depending on the level, on the zone level. There were the outpatient clinics. There were also military hospitals that fell under the jurisdiction of the General Staff, depending on the territory. I'm talking about from December to March period. It depended on the territories where they were located. A military hospital was located in territory of the Pashtrik operation zone and in Pagarusha village concretely. One was in Drenica, and in other places there were mostly clinics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: All in all, how many hospitals and clinics did the KLA have?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period from December to March. There were two military hospitals, and every zone had its clinic. I can't give you an exact number. There were seven zones; each had an ambulance. But depending on the territory or the units deployed there, there were other clinics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the soldiers of the KLA wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, they did. In 1998, there were less uniforms. Some of them didn't wear a uniform. In 1999, there were more in uniform. Almost all the soldiers were wearing uniforms. Uniforms were different because we received them from various countries, from various armies. There were camouflage and non-camouflage uniforms. Some soldiers, those who served in the logistics, wore uniforms that were similar to the military uniforms. So, as I said, in 1999, the number of soldiers in uniform was greater. The uniforms were different in terms of colours. They had the same emblem, KLA emblem, which was the same. But the uniforms, as I said, they were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how did the KLA emblem look?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The KLA emblem, you can see it in the document where my order was. Soldiers wore it on the left arm, and it read "KLA, Kosovo Liberation Army." It was red and there was a black eagle in the centre. And the same emblem was also on the cap; it was the same but smaller in size.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the -- when you said you referred to -- I think you said "my document," are you referring to the rule book?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, as you see it in the rule book. That was the emblem that soldiers wore also on their caps. The one that they wore on the left arm was bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So that was P2449, just for reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did all soldiers wear the KLA emblem?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Not all the KLA had uniforms. As I said earlier, most of them had camouflage or non-camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But those who did have a uniform, did they have an -- all have an emblem on them or ...

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: All those who wore uniforms also had the emblem on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When KLA soldiers were going on leave, for example, would they bring their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: It depended on the soldier. If he went to a territory that was not under the KLA territory, he surrendered the uniform to the command. Those who went to territories under the control of the KLA, they kept the uniform when they went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what about personal weapons?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In territories which were not controlled by KLA, they didn't take the weapons with them; especially the long rifles, they left them with the units. They could keep their pistols, but in territories controlled by the KLA they went home in full attire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we could maybe take -- stop for today here. I have a few points relating to weapons, communications, some things to tie up for tomorrow, but we could have a break here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Zyrapi, we have to finish there for today because another case occupies this courtroom this afternoon. You need to come back to continue your evidence tomorrow; that will be at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. Meanwhile, between now and then, it's extremely important that you have no discussion with anyone about your evidence. You can discuss what you like with whomsoever you like, as long as you do not, with anyone, discuss any aspect of your evidence, either the evidence you've given or the evidence you may yet give in the court. So we'll see you tomorrow at 2.15. Could you now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Until 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
